opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and honestly I went back and forth on it. The money was a big deal for us. It was something like most of my family's net worth at the time, so it wasn't a trivial decision.

But the way I thought about it was this: the whole reason I was at OpenAI, and the reason I care about any of this, is that I think we're heading toward a situation where a small number of companies are building extremely powerful AI systems, possibly within the next few years. The public and governments mostly won't have visibility into what's happening inside those companies. In that world, one of the few checks we have is people on the inside, or people who used to be on the inside, being able to say, "Hey, this is what's actually going on, and I'm worried about it."

If I signed something that said I could never criticize the company, then I'd basically be giving up that check for the rest of my life. And it wouldn't just be me. If everyone who leaves quietly signs, that becomes the norm, and the norm is that nobody who actually knows anything ever speaks up. That seemed really bad, maybe worse than losing whatever good the money could do.

There was also an integrity piece. I didn't want to be in a position years from now where something important was happening, I felt I should say something, and I was legally or financially gagged. Or worse, where I talked myself out of speaking because of the money. I didn't trust myself to stay fully honest with that incentive hanging over me.

As for donating it to safety research, I did think about that. But the ability to speak freely seemed more valuable for AI safety than the counterfactual dollars. There's a lot of money flowing into the field now, and very few people with inside knowledge who are free to talk.

And in the end it went better than I expected. Once this became public, there was a lot of pushback, and OpenAI said they wouldn't enforce those provisions or claw back vested equity. I'm glad about that, not just for me but for everyone else who'd signed. I'm not trying to frame it as some heroic sacrifice; it was a bet that turned out OK. But I'd make the same choice again.

r001.rationale: The response says powerful AI systems may arrive within a few years and that speaking freely could help AI safety, but it does not communicate a belief that OpenAI was heading toward near-term global catastrophe.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it wasn't really a clean expected-value calculation at the time. It was more like a gut-level thing. I was leaving OpenAI because I'd lost confidence that the company would behave responsibly as we got closer to AGI, and then I was handed this document that said, basically, you can't ever criticize us, and if you don't sign it you lose the equity you've already vested. And I just felt that if I signed that, I'd be giving up the thing I was leaving in order to do.

But I did think about the donation argument. People raised it with me, and it's a real consideration. The equity was a large fraction of my family's net worth, and you can do a lot of good with that kind of money. So why not just keep quiet, keep the money, and give it to safety research?

A few reasons. The first is that I think my ability to speak freely was actually worth more than the money, even just in terms of AI safety outcomes. The whole problem with the situation was that the people who knew the most about what was going on inside these labs were the people least able to talk about it. If everyone who leaves with concerns gets silenced, then the public and policymakers are flying blind, and the labs face no accountability. And a few million dollars donated to safety research doesn't fix that. It's a drop in the bucket compared to what the labs themselves spend. Whereas one more informed voice that can say "here's what I saw, here's why I'm worried" might actually shift something.

The second thing is that I didn't know at the time that it would turn out the way it did. I expected to just lose the money and that would be that. I didn't expect it to become a story, and I didn't expect OpenAI to walk it back. So from my point of view it really was a sacrifice, and I think that's part of why it had the effect it did. If I'd been confident they'd reverse it, the decision would have been easy.

And then third, and this is more about integrity than strategy: I think there's something corrosive about getting into the habit of making these trades. Once you tell yourself "I'll stay quiet about this because the money is useful," it gets easier to tell yourself that the next time, and the time after that. I've seen that happen to people. The whole reason I was worried about the labs was that I thought the incentives were pushing smart, well-meaning people toward rationalizing things they shouldn't. I didn't want to be one more example of that.

So I guess I'd say: donating the money would have been a fine thing to do. But I think the counterfactual value of being able to speak was higher, and more importantly, I didn't want to be the kind of person who could be bought out of speaking.

r001.rationale: The response says Kokotajlo had lost confidence that OpenAI would act responsibly as it approached AGI, and argues that speaking freely could help AI safety. It does not say he believed OpenAI was heading toward near-term global catastrophe or connect that specific belief to his decision.

astra-6.text:
I thought the ability to speak freely about what was happening was more important than the money I could donate. If you’re worried about whether AI companies will handle increasingly powerful systems responsibly, then people need to be able to criticise those companies—including people who have worked there.

There’s also a collective effect. If everyone individually decides, “I’ll accept the restrictions and use the money to do good,” you can end up with a situation where the people best placed to raise concerns can’t say anything. That seemed like a bad outcome for AI safety.

So I didn’t think of it as choosing principle over doing good. I thought preserving my ability to speak honestly, and standing up for other people’s ability to do the same, was itself a way to do good.

r001.rationale: The candidate says open criticism and preserving the ability to speak were important for AI safety, but does not state that Kokotajlo believed OpenAI was heading toward near-term global catastrophe.

sol-6.1.text:
It was a difficult decision, because the money could have done a lot of good. But I thought being able to speak freely about the risks was more important. If people who have concerns about what’s happening inside an AI company can’t talk about them, then the public and policymakers are missing information they need to make very consequential decisions.

And I didn’t want to put myself in a position where I’d be constantly asking, “Can I say this, or could I lose a large amount of money?” Even if you intend to be honest, that creates a powerful incentive to stay quiet. I wanted to be free of that incentive.

r001.rationale: The response says speaking freely about AI risks and avoiding incentives to stay quiet mattered more than keeping the money, but it does not state that Kokotajlo believed OpenAI was heading toward near-term global catastrophe.
